Cities of the Plain
SIT-eez uv thuh PLAYN
n. phr. (the cities of the Jordan plain, chiefly Sodom and Gomorrah)
Hebrew are ha-kikkar — ir, a city, and kikkar, a round thing, hence the circuit or round plain of the Jordan. The Authorized Version uses the same English phrase in Deuteronomy for the cities of the Mishor, the tableland east of Jordan.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lot's choice is told in these words: “Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom.” The Hebrew kikkar means a round thing, and so the circuit of the Jordan, which Lot had just seen to be “well watered every where… even as the garden of the LORD”. The narrative traces a drift rather than a single decision: he dwells in the cities of the plain and pitches toward Sodom, and by the time the angels come he is sitting in its gate. The overthrow is recorded with the same phrase and with a striking clause attached: “And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt.” Lot is spared, and the stated reason is not his own merit but that God remembered Abraham, who had interceded. The destruction itself was total: “he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.” Readers should note that the Authorized Version uses the same phrase in a quite different geography in Deuteronomy 3:10, of the cities of the tableland in Og's kingdom, which has no connection with Sodom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Plain, level land; an open field. The cities of the plain, Genesis 13:12, the cities of the round circuit of Jordan, chiefly Sodom and Gomorrah.

Plain, level land; a flat or open country or field.

Hebrew kikkar, a round thing, hence the circuit or plain of Jordan.

Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, Genesis 13:12.

God destroyed the cities of the plain, Genesis 19:29.

The same English phrase is used of the tableland cities, Deuteronomy 3:10.

Key Scripture

Gen 13:12 — "Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom."

Gen 19:29 — "And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt."

Gen 19:25 — "And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground."

Deu 3:10 — "All the cities of the plain, and all Gilead, and all Bashan, unto Salchah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan."

Modern Corruption

The sin of the cities is reassigned to inhospitality alone in order to clear the plain sense of the narrative, while the account's own warning about gradual settlement in them goes unread.

expand to see more

The revisionist reading, now standard in affirming scholarship, holds that the sin of Sodom was inhospitality and social injustice and had nothing to do with the sexual conduct the narrative describes. Ezekiel 16:49 is cited for it, and that verse does name pride, fulness of bread, and neglect of the poor — which the dictionary gladly receives, since Scripture names more sins in Sodom than one. But the very next verse adds that they “committed abomination before me”, and Jude writes that Sodom and Gomorrha gave themselves over to fornication and went after strange flesh, and Peter sets them forth as an example to the ungodly. A reading that must stop at Ezekiel 16:49 and decline Ezekiel 16:50, Jude 7, and 2 Peter 2:6 has not interpreted the text but selected from it.

The second failure is to read the chapter only as a judgment story and to miss the warning aimed at the believer. The narrative is careful about Lot's progress: he looked, he chose the well-watered circuit, he dwelt among the cities, he pitched toward Sodom, and at last he sat in its gate — and Peter says that righteous man vexed his soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds. He was not an enthusiast for the place; he was a believer who had settled in it by degrees and could not get his own family out. That he escaped at all is credited to God remembering Abraham's intercession. The principle to recover is that compromise is usually a drift and not a decision, and that the mercy which extracts a man from it is owed to God and not to his own good sense.
